paras: The attempted lynching of Sid Black was an attack near Charlotte, North Carolina, on the night of November 2, 1888, in which a crowd of Black men seized a Black man who had declared himself a Democrat, bound him, and put a rope around his neck. Other men intervened before he could be hanged, and some of the crowd were reported arrested. Papers in Richmond, New York and Durham carried the story as part of Charlotte dispatches on the political excitement before the November 6 election.

Dispatches from Charlotte dated November 3 described Mecklenburg County as more heated over politics than ever before. They reported that federal supervisors of election, many of them Black, had been appointed at the instance of O. H. Dockery, the Republican candidate for governor. The Republican state chairman, J. B. Eaves, had also announced in circular letters that Pinkerton detectives would watch the polls.

According to the Washington Evening Star and a Charlotte special to the Wilmington Messenger, Black men who announced they would vote Democratic were sent "letters of warning" decorated with a coffin and signed by the Republican Executive Committee. The letters reportedly told such men to come back to the Republican party or die before November 6.

On the night of November 2, near Charlotte, a crowd caught a Black man named Black, who had recently left the Republican party, and urged him to return to it. The Messenger's correspondent gave his name as Sid Black, described his captors as "nearly 100 armed men," and wrote that they told him he must come back "or die"; the New York Sun put the crowd at 100, while the Richmond Dispatch gave no number. When he refused, the crowd bound him hand and foot and placed a rope about his neck.

By the Dispatch and Sun accounts the men were looking for a limb to hang him from, and by the Messenger's they were preparing to carry him away, when "other parties" or "some other men" came to his rescue. None of the reports names the rescuers or says whether Black was hurt.

All three accounts said that some of the mob had been arrested, but none named them or gave the charges. No report of a hearing, indictment or trial was found, and no account from Black himself or from the men arrested appears in the coverage.

The attack reached print as a paragraph inside longer Charlotte dispatches about the campaign rather than as a report of its own. The Richmond Dispatch ran it on November 4 under the headline "Great Excitement" and the deck "Attempt to Lynch a Democratic Negro," in a special telegram that said Democrats were "terribly indignant" at Republican efforts to "play the bulldoze game." The New York Sun printed a closely similar dispatch the same day, subheaded "The White Man or the Negro is the Issue in the Turpentine State," which warned that Black Republicans in the section were "well armed."

On November 7 the Durham Recorder reprinted the Messenger's special under "At White Heat," calling the crowd "thirsty for his blood" and saying the canvass had made the issue "squarely, white men and negroes." The three versions share much of their wording, which points to a single Charlotte correspondent, and each presented the attack as an instance of Republican intimidation of Black Democrats. The Evening Star's own Charlotte dispatch of November 3 described the coffin letters but did not mention the attack.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Sid Black
bases: A crowd seized a man, bound him, put a rope about his neck and sought a limb to hang him from before others rescued him, which the Richmond Dispatch headlined an 'Attempt to Lynch' (A3, A4, A5).

Black was rescued alive, so no one was killed; the crowd (put at about 100 in A4 and A5) acted without lawful authority, but its stated demand was political, that he return to the Republican party, rather than a claim of punishing a crime (A3, A4, A5).

Three papers carried the story, but all three versions are Charlotte dispatches of Nov. 3 that share much of their wording and appear to come from one correspondent, and no independent local, Republican or court account was found (A3, A4, A5).

accounts.label: Charlotte correspondent (Richmond Dispatch telegram)
accounts.gist: A crowd of negroes caught a colored Democrat named Black, pleaded with him to return to the Republicans, then bound him, roped his neck and looked for a limb until others rescued him; some of the mob were arrested.

accounts.label: Charlotte correspondent (New York Sun)
accounts.gist: A crowd of 100 negroes caught Black, who had recently left the Republican party, near Charlotte; they bound him and looked for a limb to hang him until some other men interfered; some were arrested.

accounts.label: Charlotte special to the Wilmington Messenger
accounts.gist: Nearly 100 armed men took up Sid Black and told him to come back to the Republicans or die; they bound and roped him and were preparing to carry him away when others rescued him; some were arrested.

framing.detail: The Richmond Dispatch ran the attack under the deck 'Attempt to Lynch a Democratic Negro' inside a telegram on Democrats 'terribly indignant' at the Republican 'bulldoze game'.
The New York Sun's dispatch was subheaded 'The White Man or the Negro is the Issue in the Turpentine State' and told of armed Black Republicans and determined white men.
The Durham Recorder's reprint of the Wilmington Messenger special, 'At White Heat', called the crowd 'thirsty for his blood' and said the canvass had made the issue 'white men and negroes'.

conflicts.note: Likely variants of one correspondent's dispatch; only A5 says the men were armed.
